clinicalPearls: A midline cystic remnant of the paramesonephric (mullerian) duct, situated in or above the prostate near the midline
It does not communicate with the urethra and does not contain spermatozoa, in contrast to a prostatic utricle cyst
Often asymptomatic and found incidentally; larger cysts may cause voiding symptoms, perineal pain, ejaculatory dysfunction, haematospermia or infertility
It typically presents in the third to fourth decades as the cyst enlarges, unlike utricle cysts, which more often present in childhood
Its midline position distinguishes it from laterally placed seminal vesicle cysts
MRI and transrectal ultrasound define the midline location and the relationship to the verumontanum
Small asymptomatic cysts are observed, whereas symptomatic cysts may be aspirated, marsupialised or excised
reference.pathophysiology: Mullerian duct cysts arise from incomplete regression of the paramesonephric ducts, which in males normally involute under the influence of anti-mullerian hormone, leaving only the prostatic utricle and the appendix testis. A retained segment can dilate into a midline cyst behind the prostate that lies above the verumontanum and, unlike the utricle, does not open into the prostatic urethra.
additionalDifferentials: Prostatic utricle cyst, which is midline and communicates with the urethra
Seminal vesicle cyst, which is laterally placed
Zinner syndrome when renal agenesis is present
additionalInvestigations: Pelvic MRI to confirm the midline location and characterise the contents
Transrectal ultrasound for size and relationship to the prostate and ejaculatory ducts
Cyst fluid analysis, where absence of spermatozoa favours a mullerian rather than utricle or ejaculatory duct origin
Semen analysis if infertility is present
Cross-sectional imaging to exclude solid components or malignancy
Renal imaging to assess for associated anomalies
redFlags: Solid components or rapid growth suggesting rare malignant transformation
reference.prognosis: Benign with a favourable outcome; most remain asymptomatic and symptomatic lesions respond well to drainage or excision, with only rare reports of malignancy arising within long-standing cysts.
pitfalls: Confusing a mullerian duct cyst with a prostatic utricle cyst, when fluid spermatozoa and urethral communication help distinguish them
Mislabelling a midline cyst as a lateral seminal vesicle cyst
Overlooking rare malignant change in long-standing cysts
Attributing symptoms to benign prostatic enlargement
management: Conservative observation for small, asymptomatic cysts
Surgical excision or deroofing by a transurethral, transrectal or laparoscopic/robotic approach for symptomatic or enlarging cysts
Aspiration or drainage as a less invasive option for symptomatic relief
Management of associated voiding symptoms, ejaculatory dysfunction or haematospermia
Fertility assessment and assisted reproductive input where infertility is present
Surveillance imaging for recurrence and for the rare development of malignancy within long-standing cysts
Referral to urology and evaluation for associated renal tract anomalies
